title: Judgment on Tyre
overview: Ezekiel 26 pronounces a divine oracle against the ancient city of Tyre, a powerful Phoenician maritime center. The chapter details God's judgment through the agency of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who will bring destruction upon Tyre and its territories. The prophecy emphasizes the certainty of Tyre's downfall, the devastation of its walls and wealth, and its ultimate desolation as a rock for fishermen. This chapter highlights God's sovereignty over nations and His righteous judgment against pride and opposition to Jerusalem. It serves as a vivid example of prophetic warning and fulfillment, illustrating the consequences of defiance against God's people and plans.
structure:
**Verses 1-6: The Divine Accusation and Judgment Pronounced.** The chapter opens with God addressing Ezekiel, revealing Tyre's prideful rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall and declaring the coming judgment against Tyre and its daughters.

**Verses 7-12: The Instrument of Judgment—Nebuchadnezzar’s Siege.** God announces that Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, will lead a massive military campaign against Tyre, describing the siege tactics and destruction in vivid detail.

**Verses 13-14: The Final Desolation of Tyre.** God declares the silencing of Tyre’s songs and its transformation into a bare rock, no longer to be rebuilt, emphasizing the irrevocability of the judgment.

**Verses 15-18: The Lamentation of the Nations.** The surrounding islands and maritime princes mourn Tyre’s fall, recognizing its former strength and terror.

**Verses 19-21: The Ultimate Fate—Desolation and Eternal Terror.** The chapter concludes with a graphic depiction of Tyre’s burial beneath the waters and its permanent desolation, underscoring God’s sovereign power to erase even the mightiest cities.

keyVerses.text: And they shall destroy the walls of Tyrus, and break down her towers: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the totality of God's judgment on Tyre, symbolizing complete destruction and humiliation. It underscores God's power to reduce a proud city to nothing, reinforcing the theme of divine sovereignty over human pride.

keyVerses.text: For thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring upon Tyrus Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, a king of kings, from the north, with horses, and with chariots, and with horsemen, and companies, and much people.
keyVerses.significance: This verse identifies the human instrument of God's judgment, Nebuchadnezzar, emphasizing that earthly rulers act under divine authority. It also reflects the historical reality of Babylon’s military dominance.

keyVerses.text: And I will make thee like the top of a rock: thou shalt be a place to spread nets upon; thou shalt be built no more: for I the LORD have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD.
keyVerses.significance: This verse confirms the irrevocable nature of the prophecy, portraying Tyre’s permanent desolation. It serves as a solemn reminder that God's decrees are certain and unchangeable.

keyVerses.text: I will make thee a terror, and thou shalt be no more: though thou be sought for, yet shalt thou never be found again, saith the Lord GOD.
keyVerses.significance: This concluding verse emphasizes the complete erasure of Tyre’s existence, symbolizing the ultimate judgment and warning against opposing God’s will.

characters.name: God (The LORD)
characters.description: The sovereign judge who declares and executes judgment against Tyre. God reveals His authority over nations and history, pronouncing the downfall of Tyre due to its pride and hostility toward Jerusalem.

characters.name: Nebuchadrezzar
characters.description: King of Babylon, described as the 'king of kings' and the instrument of God's judgment against Tyre. He leads the military siege that brings destruction upon the city, fulfilling the divine prophecy.

characters.name: Tyre
characters.description: A wealthy and powerful Phoenician city-state, characterized by pride and opposition to Jerusalem. Tyre’s fall is the central focus of the chapter, symbolizing the consequences of defiance against God.

themes.description: God’s control over nations and history is central, as He orchestrates the rise and fall of empires. Tyre’s destruction demonstrates that no city or power can resist God’s will.
Tyre’s arrogance and rejoicing over Jerusalem’s fall provoke God’s wrath. The chapter illustrates the biblical principle that pride leads to downfall.
The detailed prophecy about Tyre’s destruction underscores the reliability of God’s word through His prophets, affirming that His declarations will come to pass.
The chapter reveals that God’s judgments are just responses to sin and opposition, highlighting His righteous governance over human affairs.

historicalContext: Ezekiel 26 was delivered during the early 6th century BC, a time when Babylon was expanding its empire under Nebuchadnezzar II. Tyre was a prominent Phoenician city located on the Mediterranean coast, renowned for its maritime trade and wealth. Its strategic island location made it a formidable fortress, and it had a history of political and economic rivalry with Jerusalem and Judah. The prophecy reflects the geopolitical tensions of the period, with Babylon seeking to dominate the region and punish cities that opposed or rejoiced over Judah’s downfall. The siege of Tyre, historically lasting many years, was a significant event demonstrating Babylonian military power and fulfilling Ezekiel’s prophecy.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty and justice in ordaining the rise and fall of nations. Tyre’s destruction is seen as a just punishment for pride and opposition to God’s covenant people, illustrating God’s control over history.

Dispensationalists often view this prophecy as a literal future fulfillment or as partially fulfilled historically with Nebuchadnezzar’s siege, emphasizing God’s ongoing plan for Israel and the nations. The chapter is interpreted as part of God’s judgment on Gentile powers opposing His people.

Early church interpreters often saw Tyre as a symbol of worldly pride and materialism. They interpreted the prophecy allegorically as a warning against spiritual arrogance and the eventual downfall of all earthly powers opposed to God’s kingdom.

crossReferences.connection: Isaiah also prophesies the fall of Tyre, emphasizing its wealth and destruction, paralleling Ezekiel’s oracle.
Jeremiah mentions Tyre among the nations judged by Babylon, confirming the historical context of Ezekiel’s prophecy.
The fall of Babylon in Revelation echoes the judgment themes seen in Tyre’s destruction, symbolizing the downfall of proud, worldly cities.
This psalm’s assurance of God’s protection contrasts with Tyre’s downfall, highlighting God’s sovereignty over chaos and nations.
Nebuchadnezzar is identified as God’s servant to execute His purposes, aligning with Ezekiel’s depiction of him as the instrument of judgment.

application: Recognize and submit to God’s sovereignty over all nations and circumstances in your life.
Avoid pride and arrogance, understanding that God humbles the proud and exalts the humble.
Trust in the certainty of God’s promises and warnings as revealed through His Word.
Pray for humility and repentance, especially when tempted to rejoice over others’ misfortunes.
Remember that God’s justice will ultimately prevail, encouraging perseverance in faith.
Use the example of Tyre’s downfall to examine personal attitudes toward God and others.
conclusion: Ezekiel 26 stands as a powerful testament to God’s sovereign authority over history and nations. Through the vivid prophecy of Tyre’s destruction, believers are reminded of the dangers of pride and opposition to God’s purposes. The chapter assures that God’s judgments are just and certain, and that He raises up and brings down kingdoms according to His will. For the Christian today, this chapter calls for humility, trust in God’s providence, and faithful obedience, knowing that God’s word will never fail.
timeline: c. 593 BC - Prophecy against Tyre during Ezekiel’s early prophetic ministry, shortly before the Babylonian siege.

outline.heading: Divine Judgment Pronounced on Tyre
outline.description: God reveals Tyre’s arrogance and declares that many nations will come against it, leading to its destruction and the death of its daughters.

outline.heading: Nebuchadnezzar’s Siege Described
outline.description: The Babylonian king is introduced as the instrument of God’s judgment, with detailed descriptions of the siege tactics and devastation.

outline.heading: Tyre’s Final Desolation
outline.description: God declares the silencing of Tyre’s songs and its transformation into a bare rock, never to be rebuilt.

outline.heading: The Nations’ Lament Over Tyre
outline.description: The surrounding islands and maritime rulers mourn Tyre’s fall, acknowledging its former strength and terror.

outline.heading: Eternal Judgment and Desolation
outline.description: The chapter concludes with a vivid depiction of Tyre’s burial beneath the sea and its permanent erasure as a city.
